retro.headline: Assessors will recommend a single (not split) tax rate and rejecting all three optional exemptions for FY2026
retro.summary: The Board of Assessors reviewed FY2026 valuation and growth figures, worked through mapping and MUNIS data delays, and discussed hiring a third party to redo property neighborhoods after a citizen work group flagged inconsistent boundaries. Most of the meeting was spent line-editing a classification-hearing presentation, ending in board recommendations to reject the residential, open-space, and small commercial exemptions and to keep a single tax rate, plus review of a fall town meeting exemption/COLA warrant article and website fixes.

what_happened.line: The Board of Assessors recommended a single, not split, tax rate for FY2026.
The board voted to reject adopting the residential exemption for the FY2026 classification.
The board also voted to reject adopting the small commercial exemption for FY2026.
The board leaned toward hiring an outside firm, rather than the citizen work group, to redo property-neighborhood boundaries after inconsistencies were flagged.
The assessor said the printed fall town meeting warrant article understated the cost of adopting COLA-linked exemption updates as zero and said it needs correcting before town meeting.

why_it_matters: A single versus split tax rate changes how the tax levy is divided between residential and commercial/industrial property, which shows up directly in individual tax bills.
Declining the residential and small commercial exemptions means the classification hearing will not shift additional tax burden between property types beyond the rate decision itself.

The COLA-linked exemption warrant article, once its cost is corrected, goes to voters at fall town meeting and is paid from the overlay account, meaning any expansion is funded by other taxpayers rather than the town budget.
watch_next: November 20 Board of Assessors meeting, including a planned resident outreach conference on abatements and exemptions
The fall town meeting warrant article on COLA adjustments to Clauses 41C/41D/17D/17E/17F, once its cost figure is corrected

retro.headline: APDC sent legal questions on its demolition bylaw to executive session amid a push to merge with the Historical Commission
retro.summary: The Architectural Preservation District Commission welcomed the town's new land use director, approved prior minutes, and spent most of the meeting on a proposed merger with the Historical Commission, moving unresolved legal questions about the APD bylaw's enforceability to executive session. Members also discussed the troubled Ritter/Town Hall renovation design process, agreed to digitize the determination-of-applicability form via OpenGov.com, and reviewed building-repair, Brooks house, and cemetery-restoration project updates.

what_happened.line: The commission sent open legal questions about the demolition bylaw's enforceability into executive session amid a push to merge with the Historical Commission.
Members leaned toward merging the two boards into one, while keeping the historic district's current boundaries, pending legal review.
A member was tasked with drafting bylaw and design-guideline changes for the merger to bring back in February, after the chair pulls the bylaw's Attorney General review file.
The commission agreed to move its determination-of-applicability form onto the town's OpenGov.com system.
The next meeting was set for February 13.

why_it_matters: A merger would change which board reviews demolition and renovation requests inside the Architectural Preservation District, and the bylaw's enforceability is itself in question.
watch_next: February 13 meeting, when drafted bylaw and design-guideline changes for the merger return
the Attorney General review file on the APD bylaw

retro.headline: Committee voted to hire Rich Matthew as director of finance and operations, pending contract; requested $300,000 free cash for special ed reserve.
retro.summary: The School Committee publicly interviewed a finance director candidate and voted unanimously to hire him pending contract negotiations. It also approved FY27 line item transfers, surplus literacy materials, a 0.5 OT position change, the paraprofessional contract, and a request for special education reserve funding. Discussion covered MCAS and DIBELS results, Brooks House, and track and field turf costs.

what_happened.line: The School Committee voted unanimously to hire a director of finance and operations, pending contract negotiations, after a public interview.
The Committee voted unanimously to request free cash for the special education reserve fund, if certified at the November town meeting.
The Committee voted unanimously to accept new terms of the paraprofessional contract.
Members voted unanimously to accept FY27 line item transfers and to change a previously voted position to a 0.5 position.
A member said track and field drainage and wall repairs appear to cost about a million dollars before turf; no vote was taken.

why_it_matters: The free cash request rides on the November town meeting warrant article, so residents at that meeting will be asked to certify the money that funds the special education reserve.
The new finance director and the new paraprofessional contract terms shape who prepares the school budget and what a staffing line costs in coming budgets.
Track and field costs have no resolution yet, so a capital request may reach residents later.
watch_next: The November town meeting, where free cash for the special education reserve is to be certified.
The next School Committee meeting, where facilities staff are to present steps and a timeline for the track and field project.

retro.headline: Commission approved several septic and other compliance certificates and two NOIs, and continued most hearings to October 21.
retro.summary: The Conservation Commission heard a planning director presentation on four draft zoning amendments, then worked through a long hearing list. Most hearings were continued to October 21; the Sunny Hill Road driveway, the Goodrich Street irrigation pond and the Pleasant Street septic were approved. The commission also approved eight certificates of compliance and authorized spending on the Hollis Road house.

what_happened.line: The commission approved three notices of intent: a driveway crossing at Sunny Hill Road, an irrigation pond on Goodrich Street, and a septic replacement on Pleasant Street.
Most other hearings were continued to October 21, including 3 Wilderwood Avenue, 37 Fire Road 10, 386 Sunset Lane, 143 Island Road, 404 Page Street, and the Mass Ave sites.
The commission approved certificates of compliance for properties on Sunset Lane, Island Road, Laurel Lane, Beiel Street and White Street, each by 5-0.
For the Hollis Road house, the commission approved a flooring proposal paid from the Hollis Road account and capped paint and supplies spending.
The planning director presented four draft zoning amendments, with comments due at the end of November.

why_it_matters: Approved notices of intent set the conditions for work near wetlands in town, and the continued hearings on Wilderwood, Fire Road and Sunset Lane stay open to public comment on October 21.
The draft zoning amendments on senior housing, inclusionary, cluster and minor site plan rules could change what can be built in town, and residents can still comment before the end of November.
Hollis Road house repairs are drawing on a dedicated commission account, and a plan to put a caretaker on the town payroll would need a town meeting article that residents would vote on.
watch_next: October 21: continued hearings resume, including 3 Wilderwood Avenue, 37 Fire Road 10 and 386 Sunset Lane.
End of November: deadline for comments on the four draft zoning amendments.

retro.headline: Board set Lunenburg Middle High gym as Nov 3 polling place and put several articles on the Nov 17 warrant.
retro.summary: The Select Board granted a common victualler license to Kiku Asian Cuisine, re-voted the polling location after the cafeteria proved too small, and discussed the future of the tri-board and bylaw cleanup for committees. It reviewed the November 17 special town meeting warrant, including several articles and holds for later. The board also discussed municipal building consolidation, a personnel committee liaison, and an early voting location agreement.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted unanimously to hold the Nov 3 election at the Lunenburg Middle High School gymnasium, after the cafeteria proved too small.

The board voted unanimously to put the omnibus budget amendment, a prior-year bill payment, the special education reserve transfer, zoning corrections and the stormwater fee article on the Nov 17 warrant.
The board held several articles off the warrant for now, including track and field engineering, veterans exemptions, the PEG Access fund, trust funds and classification plan changes.
The board voted unanimously to put a non-binding question on the TC Passios demolition on the warrant.
The board left the tri-board's future open and will seek a joint meeting with the municipal building design committee before special town meeting.

why_it_matters: Residents voting Nov 3 should go to the gym, not the cafeteria, and the Nov 17 special town meeting warrant now lists the articles they will be asked to vote on.
The special education reserve transfer and the budget amendment draw on town money, and the held track and field engineering article may return after the finance committee hearing.
watch_next: Special town meeting on Nov 17, with a possible joint meeting with the municipal building design committee on Monday Nov 2.
The held articles, including track and field engineering, which the board tied to the finance committee hearing and a presentation.

retro.headline: School Committee unanimously approved a new director of finance and operations title and hired a temporary director.
retro.summary: A short meeting with two items. The committee voted to change the business administrator job description and title to director of finance and operations, adding facilities, technology, transportation, athletics and food service duties. It then approved a retired finance official as temporary director, three days a week, to close out FY26 and build FY27. The superintendent also reported the new athletic director gave 30 days' notice.

what_happened.line: The School Committee voted unanimously, by roll call, to retitle the business administrator job as director of finance and operations.
The new title adds facilities, technology, transportation, athletics and food service duties to the role.
The committee voted unanimously to approve a temporary director of finance and operations, available three days a week, to close out FY26 and build FY27.
The superintendent is to prepare the temporary director's contract; if a permanent director is hired, the temporary director would overlap for cleanup and the FY28 budget build.
The superintendent reported the athletic director resigned on 30 days' notice, and a half-time athletic director position has been posted.

why_it_matters: The person who prepares and presents the school budget is changing, with an interim in place for the FY26 close-out and FY27 work and a permanent hire not yet made, so the FY28 budget build may be done by someone new.

The broader title puts facilities, technology, transportation, athletics and food service under one finance-and-operations role, and the minutes say the duties were widened to match a higher salary, which touches the administration side of the school budget.
watch_next: Next School Committee meeting, Wednesday, October 7, expected to run longer.
The temporary director's contract, which the superintendent is to prepare.

retro.headline: Board designated the middle-high school cafeteria as polling place and ratified a new fire chief and police officer.
retro.summary: After an executive session on the fire chief, the Select Board voted on the polling location, a police officer appointment, an earth removal renewal, a car dealer license, an open meeting law response, the fire chief contract and an appointment policy. It also reviewed handbook chapters, discussed warrant articles for the special town meeting, and heard committee reports.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted 4-0 to designate the middle school cafeteria as the polling place, contingent on an accessibility study.
The board ratified the employment agreement for the fire chief, running from the current chief's retirement to mid-2029; the vote was unanimous.
The board accepted the findings in an open meeting law response letter and authorized the chair to sign and submit it, unanimously.
The board ratified a full-time police officer appointment, approved an earth removal renewal, and granted a class 2 auto dealer license, all unanimously.
The board adopted a revised appointment policy as amended, then discussed the special town meeting warrant without settling its articles.

why_it_matters: The polling place decision sets where residents vote, though registrars asked that the general election be held at TC Pacios rather than a school and the designation depends on an accessibility study.

Items discussed for the special town meeting warrant, including school-side funding requests and a possible transfer of free cash to a special education reserve, are ones residents may be asked to vote on, with amounts not yet set.
watch_next: Stormwater and school committee presentations on October 20, and handbook chapters 1-6 returning at the next meeting.
The town manager's walkthrough of the school cafeteria with the superintendent, and the accessibility study the polling place vote depends on.

retro.headline: Chair refused a commissioner's PFAS/manganese cost-saving proposal presentation, deferring it to next meeting.
retro.summary: The Water District Commissioners discussed IT/cybersecurity costs, adopted an informal policy requiring commissioners to give advance notice before adding substantive items to the agenda, and voted to put water-quality (PFAS/manganese) data on the district website. The bulk of the meeting was a heated dispute over whether a commissioner could present, that day, a proposal to avoid a roughly $40 million treatment plant by blending well water; the chair deferred it to the next meeting pending input from DEP, and the district also reported progress on the Metal Lane/Rolling Acres water main project.

what_happened.line: The chair declined to let a commissioner present his plan to blend well water instead of building a new treatment plant, deferring it to the next meeting pending state DEP input.
Commissioners voted to post the district's manganese and PFAS testing data and charts on its website, updated at least quarterly.
The board set an informal rule that a commissioner must request an agenda item through the clerk-treasurer in advance rather than raise it the day of a meeting.
A commissioner argued the standard PFAS/manganese treatment approach carries a large capital cost plus an ongoing annual operating cost, and said well-blending could avoid both if DEP approves it.

why_it_matters: Which treatment path the district picks for PFAS and manganese -- a new plant or well-blending -- will set the size of a capital project that ratepayers eventually finance through water rates.
Public posting of the water-quality data lets residents check manganese and PFAS levels themselves rather than take the board's word for it.
The new advance-notice rule for agenda items changes how a commissioner or resident gets a substantive proposal in front of the board on a given meeting date.
watch_next: Next Water District meeting: the well-blending proposal, circulated by email beforehand, comes back for discussion
A DEP meeting expected around October on whether well-blending is a viable alternative to the treatment plant

retro.headline: Assessors tabled a plan to expand veterans' property-tax exemptions until the chair weighs in
retro.summary: The Board of Assessors, missing its chair for the whole meeting, covered office relocation, an unfilled data-collector position, ongoing neighborhood/site-index revaluation work with a consultant, and preparations for a tax classification hearing tentatively set for November 17. It also discussed two warrant articles that would expand and CPI-index veterans' property tax exemptions but voted to table that discussion until the chair could take part, and closed by scheduling a special meeting for September 30 and entering executive session.

what_happened.line: The board tabled draft warrant articles expanding veterans' property-tax exemptions until the chair, absent all meeting, can take part.
A special meeting was set for September 30 specifically to take up and possibly vote on that exemption language with the chair present.
The assessor was asked to prepare individual, outlier-level home value changes rather than only group averages, ahead of a tax classification hearing.
The board is trying to set a tax classification hearing for November 17, coordinated with the Select Board, with backup dates in reserve.
Approval of executive-session minutes was pushed to September 30 because they had not yet been printed.

why_it_matters: A change to veterans' exemptions affects who qualifies for tax relief and, since the town covers the cost above the state reimbursement cap, how much is absorbed by other taxpayers.

The tax classification hearing sets how the overall tax burden splits between residential and commercial/industrial property, and the individual (not just averaged) value data will show whether some homeowners see increases well above the town-wide figure.
Residents following the veterans exemption proposal or worried about a sharp assessment increase on their own home will not see a decision until the chair returns.

retro.headline: Conservation Commission approved the Lake Shirley boat ramp rebuild with wetland buffer waivers.
retro.summary: The Lunenburg Conservation Commission held a long session covering multiple RDAs, NOIs, tree-removal determinations and a certificate of compliance, approving several routine wetland-adjacent projects (a cemetery expansion, septic repairs, a shed/sand permit, tree removals) with standard conditions. The major substantive action was approval of the Shady Point boat ramp reconstruction on Lake Shirley with buffer-zone waivers after public debate over impervious-surface classification and a retaining wall versus riprap; several other hearings (404 Page Street, 108 Sunny Hill Road, the Violet irrigation pond, 141 Pleasant Street) were continued to October 7. The commission also discussed Hollis Road residence budget items, a storm water utility warrant article, and a resolved no-trespass situation at the Pleasant Street Conservation Area.

what_happened.line: The commission approved the Lake Shirley boat ramp rebuild at Shady Point, granting waivers to work inside the normal 30-foot no-disturb and 50-foot no-build wetland buffers.
Four other wetland hearings, including a new house and driveway at 404 Page Street, were continued to October 7 rather than decided.
The commission approved three routine RDAs with standard conditions: a DPW cemetery expansion, a septic force main repair, and a shed/sand permit.
A non-binding warrant article was finalized asking whether storm water funding should move out of the operating budget into a dedicated storm water utility.
A vote on replacing flooring at the town-owned Hollis Road residence was deferred pending clarification of a vendor's deposit request.

why_it_matters: The boat ramp decision sets a precedent for allowing construction inside protected wetland buffers along Lake Shirley when a project shows a public benefit.

The storm water warrant article, if it reaches town meeting, would ask voters to decide whether storm water work gets its own dedicated funding stream instead of competing inside the general operating budget.
Residents near 404 Page Street, 108 Sunny Hill Road, the Violet irrigation pond, and 141 Pleasant Street will have another chance to be heard before any of those projects are decided.
watch_next: October 7, 2026: continued hearings for 404 Page Street, 108 Sunny Hill Road, the Violet irrigation pond, and 141 Pleasant Street
The storm water utility warrant article, as submitted for an upcoming town meeting

The stormwater bylaw change would tie fee amounts to a planning-board schedule that can change without a town meeting vote, which residents will be asked to weigh in November.

Stormwater Task Force, Monday September 14: Task force approved its stormwater warrant article for special town meeting by unanimous roll call.

• The task force voted unanimously by roll call to accept its stormwater warrant article, with town counsel's edits, for the special town meeting.
• The approved article is to go out that night to town staff for filing ahead of the meeting.
• Members are working to schedule presentations to FinCom, the Select Board, and a public information session before the November 17 town meeting.
• The next task force meeting, September 21, will finalize what those presentations say about the budget and the funding-mechanism options.

Why it matters: This sends a stormwater program to a warrant article residents will vote on at the November 17 special town meeting. How the program is funded -- a utility-style fee versus a blended approach -- changes how costs split between the town, commercial and industrial properties, which can show up as a bill. FinCom and Select Board presentations, still being scheduled, are where that funding-mechanism choice gets debated before the vote.

Watch next: Special town meeting, November 17, where the warrant article goes to a vote; FinCom presentation, targeted for October 22.

Votes taken (1): Accept the warrant article for special town meeting with the changes from town counsel — passed (roll call: Jenny I, Renee I, John I, Tim I).
